records.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
records.summary:
Turks and Caicos decriminalised same-sex activity in 2001 through the UK-imposed Caribbean reform, and its constitution now bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The live frontier has been recognition rather than criminal law: the Court of Appeal ordered a residence permit for the same-sex spouse lawfully married abroad, holding that 'spouse' in the immigration ordinance must include same-sex spouses and declaring violations of the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees — while declining to touch the constitution's male-female marriage definition, which it treated as controlling.

The administering state's passport guidance maintains a standing profile of the territory's rules on marriage, civil partnerships, adoption and gender recognition. Socially, a resident's account described 'virtually nothing' documented about gay life — in a territory where around two-thirds of inhabitants are themselves not native-born — so visitor experience runs on privacy and the resort economy rather than any visible scene.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz 'Being Gay in Turks & Caicos Islands' (May 2009): a resident's account - like 2/3 of the population he is not originally from TCI; the Belonger (full-citizen) population is a demographic minority versus foreigners; 'virtually nothing on the Internet about gay life in TCI'.

UK HM Passport Office Knowledge Base profile for Turks and Caicos Islands (updated April 2025): nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, and documents - official UK guidance on the territory's legal framework.

TC Weekly News: landmark Court of Appeal ruling ordered a residence permit for Richard Sankar's same-sex spouse Timothy Haymon - 'spouse' in the Immigration Ordinance must include a same-sex spouse lawfully married elsewhere; violations of equality (s.7), non-discrimination (s.16) and private/family life (s.9) declared; but the court declined to change marriage law, citing the constitution's man-woman marriage definition (s.10) as lex specialis.
Klshepedia (Wikipedia-derived): LGBTQ rights in the Turks and Caicos Islands - same-sex activity legal since 2001; sexual-orientation discrimination constitutionally banned.

records.name: Chad
records.summary: Chad is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (misdemeanour, up to 2 years); junta-adjacent governance; no LGR; no community infrastructure; very thin data.

sources.claim: US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Chad: official assessment - the 2017 Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct; significant societal stigma; no prosecutions reported.
US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Chad (archived): pre-criminalisation baseline - no law against homosexuality at the time; general human-rights context.
US State Department 2006 Human Rights Report for Chad: documents the Deby regime's abuses - extrajudicial killings, torture, MINURCAT withdrawal - general context.

HuffPost/GroundTruth Project (June 2015): 'Anti-LGBT Groups Making Inroads Across East Africa' - while further criminalisation failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda, it succeeded in Chad and Nigeria - US evangelical influence on African anti-gay laws.

records.name: Togo
records.summary: Togo is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “immodest or unnatural acts” (3 years); limited recent enforcement evidence but documented discrimination and violence; no LGR.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Togo's criminalisation of same-sex activity (up to 3 years' imprisonment under the penal code).

Afrique Arc-En-Ciel Togo + Synergía alternative report (June 2021) to the UN Human Rights Committee's 132nd session: AAEC (founded 2007) fights HIV in MSM-TG populations and documents human-rights violations across Togo and francophone West Africa; legal and judicial support for victims, advocacy, capacity building.
US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Togo: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (Article 88); societal discrimination; no legal protections.
Washington Blade (Aug 2015): 'Voices from LGBT Catholics in Western Africa' - the experiences of LGBT Catholics in the region including Togo.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Togo: documents security-force torture, impunity, and 'official and societal discrimination... against members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for Togo: significant issues include cruel treatment, harsh prisons, arbitrary detention, criminal libel enforcement, and 'crimes involving violence or threats of violence targeting lesbian, gay, bisexual...' persons.

records.name: Thailand
records.summary:
Thailand is one of Asia's most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (the kathoey tradition long predates modern categories), the state actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in Southeast Asia, and the Immigration Bureau runs a dedicated "Welcome Pride" initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 Gender Equality Act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a Thai trans woman in Pattaya highlighted — Thailand has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly Thailand's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.

sources.claim: Thai Government Public Relations Department (Aug 2024): the Immigration Bureau launched the 'Welcome Pride by Immigration' campaign to ease concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ visitors whose passports don't match their appearance or gender - travellers are advised to bring alternative documents (driver's licence, citizen ID, medical records) and biometric data is recorded; in effect since 1 August 2024 at five major international airports; part of positioning Thailand for World Pride 2030.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Thailand became the first Southeast Asian country to legalise same-sex marriage (effective 22 January 2025, gender-neutral terms, adoption and inheritance rights); the 2015 Gender Equality Act prohibits discrimination against persons 'of a different appearance from his/her own sex by birth' but allows religious/security exemptions; never colonised.

Bangkok Post (June 2025): gender recognition law is the 'next big step' in Thailand - advocates urge the government to expedite a gender-recognition law; public education is an important part of expanding rights protection (panel at the Bangkok Post 'Pride in Action' forum).

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Nov 2025): gay marriage but no hate-crime laws - Thai LGBTQ+ activists see a gap; when a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya in April, the community called it a hate crime, but Thai law has no 'hate crime' designation - bias-motivated violence is treated as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties or data collection.

Globe (May 2025): trans people in Thailand still live without legal protection - following the killing of a Thai trans woman by a Chinese citizen; despite social visibility, legal protections are absent.

HRW report 'People Can't Be Fit into Boxes' (Dec 2021): Thailand's need for legal gender recognition - decades as a destination for gender-affirming care and a reputation for safety, but no route to legal documentation matching gender identity; existing affirmative policies (e.g. first-name change) leave discretionary power with officials; social acceptance is no substitute for legal protection.

NZZ in English (May 2025): in Thailand, a culture of compromise has boosted transgender rights - the conservative government introduced progressive trans laws including free hormone treatments with little opposition; trans people experience greater societal acceptance and hold higher company positions than often true in the West; activists progressed through compromises and economic arguments (e.g. LGBTQ+ tourism).

LegalClarity overview (June 2026): Thailand offers accessible trans healthcare but meaningful gaps remain - no mechanism to change the sex marker on birth certificate, national ID or passport (title prefixes locked to sex at birth); the Name Act B.E. 2505 (1962) offers a partial workaround; marriage equality arrived January 2025 and anti-discrimination law since 2015, but no legal gender recognition.

Fulcrum (June 2025): positioning Thailand as an LGBTQ+ tourism hub - opportunities and challenges; the government's promotion of queer tourism alongside marriage equality is a strategic economic embrace, raising the question of whether it reflects genuine commitment to the local queer community or is largely mercenary.
GAM Legal Alliance (Thai law firm): overview of the post-same-sex-marriage legal landscape in Thailand - marriage, immigration, and related legal services context for LGBTQ people.

GlobalGayz archive of Thailand news and reports (2007): the National Human Rights Commission, activists seeking gay rights in the new constitution, 'Gays to get equal status under new Thai charter', Thailand considering a law allowing transsexuals to claim their adopted gender title, 'Please call me Miss' - transgender Thais, and Peter Jackson's archive of Thai gay culture and literature.

records.name: Tajikistan
records.summary:
Tajikistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation (IPHR 2024) shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition (a medicalised registration route exists on paper under the Civil Status Acts law), no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids + registry practices + zero recourse make discovery dangerous.

sources.claim: IPHR report 'Rights for All? LGBTIQ Persons in Tajikistan Systematically Denied Human Rights' (Feb 2024): documents widespread homophobia/transphobia, human-rights violations, the 2016 police register of LGBTIQ people, 2022/2023 police raids with forced HIV-testing and arbitrary criminal charges, ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police, privacy violations followed by 'pornography' prosecutions, and additional problems facing trans people.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex acts not criminalised since independence; no SOGISC non-discrimination protections; no transparent legal gender recognition procedure, though at least two trans men and one trans woman changed markers via court in 2023; nonconsensual intersex interventions legal; in 2024 ECOM recorded 27 cases of human-rights violations against LGBT people, with police arbitrary arrests, blackmail and extortion.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention/treatment and HRT across the EECA region (with country coordinators including Tajikistan), including information for trans migrants.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, Tajikistan chapter (covering 2024): Russia's anti-LGBTI laws have influenced Tajikistan; coming out risks family shame leading to sham marriages - one person was beaten, tied up without food and forcibly married, with police taking no action; in Sughd, 10+ cases of police luring LGBT people into fake meetings to register them in a database and extort money; the 2022 anti-discrimination law dropped SOGI, leaving only 'sex'.

ECOM legislative analysis (2020): 'Legislative analysis related to SOGI and HIV in Tajikistan' - identifies legal barriers for gay men, other MSM and trans people, analysing legislation and law-enforcement practice against international standards, with local partners.

HRW World Report 2017, Tajikistan chapter: the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016 - opposition leaders sentenced, lawyers imprisoned, a predetermined referendum allowing President Rahmon to rule for life - the repressive context for LGBT life.

Global Voices (Jan 2013) by Alexander Sodiqov: 'Tajikistan Remains Hell for Gays' - despite decriminalisation 15 years earlier, there is very little tolerance; those who come out become targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police; the LGBT community remains 'one of the most closed and secretive parts of Tajik society'; sparked by a violent university incident.

records.name: Turkmenistan
records.summary:
Turkmenistan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 2 years under Article 135) and, more fundamentally, Turkmenistan is one of the world's most closed states: the state exerts strict media control and heavy internet monitoring, no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible since 2019, and asylum is the community's most urgent need (ILGA-Europe). Amnesty has documented systematic abuses. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, no recourse, and no visibility — the only safe strategy is total concealment.

For a visitor: any discoverable online presence or visible nonconformity is dangerous in a state that monitors communications pervasively.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Turkmenistan: asylum remains one of the most urgent needs for the LGBTI community; the only documented research on LGBTI issues dates to 2019 (data collection almost impossible due to safety risks); Amnesty documented systemic discrimination; the April 2022 Criminal Code kept 'sodomy' provisions and increased the severity and scope of punishments; torture and inhumane treatment by law enforcement reported, with several LGBTI people forced to flee; the Ministry of National Security collaborates with regional AIDS centres, exposing HIV-test data.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Turkmenistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Article 135 (up to 2 years); societal stigma; the totalitarian state's pervasive repression.

EHPV (Estonian Network of People Living with HIV) mid-term UPR submission (2020) on Turkmenistan: LGBT persons and PLHIV 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; Article 135 criminalises consensual same-sex acts; LGBT persons are increasingly fleeing to the EU to seek refuge.

ECOM Legal Environment Assessment (2019, with Turkmen.news): legislative analysis related to LGBT rights and HIV in Turkmenistan - identifies legal barriers for PLHIV, gay men, MSM and trans people, analysing law-enforcement practice and international recommendations.
Columbia Law School (May 2007): the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured asylum for a Turkmen woman who feared persecution because she is a lesbian in the mostly Muslim country.

Goldberg Kohn (Sept 2019): attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared persecution including imprisonment and torture; homosexuality is punishable by up to 2 years; suspects face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals; women are vulnerable to sexual violence and 'honor killings'.

records.name: Timor-Leste
records.summary: Timor-Leste is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's equality provisions have been read inclusively, and Dili hosts an annual Pride march with government participation — remarkable for a young, Catholic-majority nation. There is no legal gender recognition and services are thin, but there is no documented pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence, and the small community (CODIVA, Arco Iris) operates openly.

sources.claim: Australian Volunteers Program Pride Guide for Timor-Leste: country snapshot of the local LGBTQIA+ context - same-sex acts decriminalised in 1975; the 2011 UN HRC joint statement on SOGI adopted; practical guidance for volunteers on local law, protections and living openly.

US Mission in Geneva (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - US diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the Human Rights Council, relevant to Timor-Leste's international human-rights environment.

New Naratif (June 2018) by Sophie Raynor: 'Behind Timor-Leste's Pride' - the first-ever Pride parade (2017) garnered international attention and a televised PM endorsement, but 'the shine of a single event belies a grittier day-to-day'; organiser Natalino Guterres received 'Gay people are monsters' messages from his own brother - rejection and reconciliation within families.

VOA (July 2018): Asia's youngest nation held its second LGBT pride parade - Timor-Leste cemented its role as a regional LGBT rights leader while neighbours Indonesia and Malaysia turn hostile; PM Rui Maria de Araujo: 'discrimination, disrespect and abuse toward people, because of their sexual orientation or gender identity, does not provide any benefit to our nation.'

Star Observer (July 2019): East Timor celebrated its third LGBTQI Pride - ~3,000 people joined the 'Marsa Diversidade' in Dili, six times the 2017 turnout; President Francisco Guterres: 'I am a President for all people!... I ask everyone to see diversity as our nation's wealth'; homosexuality legal since 1975.

records.name: Tonga
records.summary: Tonga demands real caution from trans visitors. The Criminal Offences Act criminalises sodomy (10 years, plus corporal punishment on paper — unenforced in recent years) and also criminalises males “impersonating a female” while soliciting — a direct trans-expression statute on the books. Against that: Tonga has a visible leiti (trans-feminine) community with the famous Miss Galaxy pageant (documented by the Washington Post in 2024), family and church networks that are devout but not systematically violent, and no documented recent prosecutions.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the Criminal Offences Act outlaws same-sex activity (max 10 years, no recent enforcement evidence) and criminalises male 'impersonation' of a female for an 'immoral purpose'; no gender recognition; intersex people unprotected; traditionally supportive culture of fakaleiti/fakafefine ('like a lady'), though rising conservatism threatens this.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (timeout); the underlying Washington Post piece (Aug 2024) covers Tonga's trans pageant and LGBT rights.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Tonga: domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption were the most prevalent problems; no reports of government abuses; the LGBT section notes the criminalisation of sodomy but rare enforcement.
Washington Blade (Feb 2018): Cyclone Gita seriously damaged Tonga's LGBTI centre and shelter - the community hub serving leiti and LGBTI Tongans.

US Mission in Geneva (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - US diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the Human Rights Council, relevant to Tonga's international human-rights environment.
UK Foreign Travel Advice for Tonga, Local Laws and Customs: official guidance for travellers including local legal customs - relevant to LGBT visitors.
